(CNN) -- The U.S. Coast Guard on Thursday is searching for two fishermen missing after a commercial fishing vessel went down in remote, treacherous waters off the Aleutian Islands about 1,400 miles southwest of Anchorage, Alaska. The fishing vessel Courageous helps search for missing men in waters off Alaska. Four of the boat's crew members were rescued and five bodies retrieved Wednesday near the Amchitka Pass, a strait that connects the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The names have been withheld pending the notification of families, a Coast Guard statement said. "What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the boat. He told The Associated Press, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead and are praying that those that are still in the water are alive." The Seattle-based company told the AP the survivors were Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster and Harold Attling. The search began at about 1 a.m. Wednesday when the Coast Guard received an emergency signal from the Katmai, a 93-foot fishing vessel that had been battling 50-knot winds and nearly 20-foot waves. The signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device on the Katmai that reacts when it's touched or splashed with water, Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read said.  Watch a "Deadliest Catch" captain talk about what may have happened on the rough seas » . At about that time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, sent an e-mail to the Coast Guard saying that it received a message from the Katmai that water was flooding its rear compartment. The message also said that the vessel had lost steering. The Coast Guard tried to e-mail the Balard back but received no response, likely because the seas are remote and Internet access can be spotty, Read said. Rescuers launched a C-130, a long-range surveillance aircraft, and went straight to the scene twice Wednesday morning, Read said. The boat was nowhere in sight, but the C-130 did spot two strobe lights on top of the water, he said. By this time, the weather was treacherous and the sky was darkening, according to Read. The C-130, having found no signs of life, dropped two life rafts and headed back, he said. On the second trip, at 11 a.m., the C-130 and a Jayhawk helicopter found two strobe lights floating in the water, one attached to a survival suit and the other to the emergency device that had first alerted the Coast Guard, Read said. They also found a body, he said. "We knew the person was from the Katmai because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said. Roughly five hours later, the Coast Guard spotted four men on a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of other vessels, the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, the bodies of four other men were recovered from the water, all wearing survival suits, Read said. The odds of someone surviving the frigid waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands is minimal, said Read. Crews usually have survival suits that allow water to seep inside but have a mechanism that traps body heat. The search for the two remaining men began at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday, an hour before sunrise there. "You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It's darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really out there."

The fishing vessel Courageous is among those assisting in the search for the missing men. Four crew members were rescued and five bodies recovered Wednesday near the Amchitka Pass, a strait connecting the Bering Sea to the Pacific Ocean. The names of those involved have been withheld pending notification of their families, according to a Coast Guard statement.

"What can you say?" said Jeff DeBell, chief financial officer of Katmai Fisheries, which owned the vessel. He told The Associated Press, "We are devastated by what has happened. We are elated there have been survivors. We are just terribly saddened by the ones that are dead, and are praying that those still in the water are alive."

The Seattle-based company confirmed to the AP that the survivors are Capt. Henry Blake and crew members Guy Schroeder, Adam Foster, and Harold Attling.

The search began around 1 a.m. Wednesday, when the Coast Guard received an emergency distress signal from the Katmai, a 93-foot fishing vessel battling 50-knot winds and waves nearly 20 feet high. The signal originated from a wall-mounted satellite positioning device aboard the Katmai that activates upon contact or exposure to water, said Coast Guard Petty Officer Levi Read.

Watch a "Deadliest Catch" captain discuss what may have happened in the rough seas »

Around the same time, another vessel, the Blue Balard, sent an e-mail to the Coast Guard reporting that it had received a message from the Katmai indicating water was flooding its rear compartment and that the vessel had lost steering. The Coast Guard attempted to respond via e-mail but received no reply — likely due to the remoteness of the area and unreliable Internet access, Read explained.

Rescuers deployed a C-130 long-range surveillance aircraft, which made two trips to the scene Wednesday morning. Though the vessel itself was nowhere in sight, the aircraft spotted two strobe lights on the water's surface. By then, the weather had grown increasingly severe and darkness was falling, according to Read. Finding no signs of life, the C-130 dropped two life rafts before returning to base.

On its second trip, at 11 a.m., the C-130, along with a Jayhawk helicopter, located two strobe lights floating in the water — one attached to a survival suit, the other to the emergency beacon that had first alerted the Coast Guard. They also discovered a body. "We knew the person was from the Katmai because the suit he was wearing had the name of the vessel on it," Read said.

About five hours later, the Coast Guard located four men aboard a life raft, all wearing survival suits. With the assistance of two other vessels, the Courageous and the Patricia Lee, four additional bodies — all clad in survival suits — were recovered from the water, Read said.

The odds of surviving the frigid waters off Alaska's Aleutian Islands are slim, Read noted. Crew members typically wear survival suits designed to allow a small amount of water inside while trapping body heat to stave off hypothermia.

The search for the two remaining fishermen resumed at 9:30 a.m. Alaska time Thursday — an hour before sunrise. "You just couldn't do anything earlier," Read said. "It gets darker the farther out you go, and they are really, really far out there."

Along America's shorelines, dramatic changes are unfolding that have captured the attention of journalists, scientists, and coastal communities alike. CNN's ongoing coverage of coastal issues explores the complex challenges facing these vital regions.

## Rising Concerns

The coast represents one of the most dynamic and vulnerable environments on our planet. From the rocky shores of Maine to the sandy beaches of California, coastal areas face unprecedented pressures from climate change, rising sea levels, and increased storm intensity. CNN correspondents have documented how these forces are reshaping communities that have existed along the water's edge for generations.

## Communities at the Edge

Coastal towns and cities represent more than just geographic locations—they embody unique cultures, economies, and ways of life built around the relationship between land and sea. Fishing villages, resort towns, and major port cities all share a common vulnerability to the changing conditions along the coast.

Local residents interviewed by news teams often express a deep connection to their coastal homes, even as they grapple with difficult questions about the future. Property values, insurance costs, and infrastructure investments all factor into decisions about whether to stay, adapt, or relocate.

## Looking Forward

As coverage continues, the story of the coast remains one of resilience and adaptation. Engineers propose innovative solutions like living shorelines and elevated construction. Policymakers debate funding for infrastructure improvements. Scientists continue monitoring changes to help communities prepare for what lies ahead.

The narrative of America's coastline is still being written, with each high tide and storm season adding new chapters to this ongoing story of environmental change and human adaptation.

# Coast Guard Searches for Survivors After Fishing Vessel Sinks Near Aleutian Islands

**By CNN Staff**

The U.S. Coast Guard is conducting an extensive search and rescue operation in the frigid waters near Alaska's Aleutian Islands after a commercial fishing vessel sank early Wednesday, according to officials.

The vessel, identified as a mid-sized crab fishing boat operating in the Bering Sea, sent out a distress signal around 3:15 a.m. local time before losing contact with Coast Guard Sector Juneau, said Petty Officer 1st Class Sarah Reeves.

"We received an EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) activation approximately 40 miles southwest of Unalaska," Reeves said. "Crews were dispatched immediately given the extreme conditions in that area."

## Harsh Conditions Complicate Search

Coast Guard officials say the search is being hampered by rough seas, sub-freezing water temperatures, and limited visibility — conditions common to the treacherous waters of the North Pacific during winter months.

"Water temperatures in that region typically hover around 38 to 40 degrees Fahrenheit this time of year," said Lt. Cmdr. Daniel Wu, a Coast Guard search and rescue coordinator. "Survival time without proper cold-water gear can be limited to a matter of hours, which is why we've mobilized every available asset."

Two Coast Guard cutters, a C-130 Hercules aircraft, and an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter have been deployed to the search area. Good Samaritan vessels operating nearby have also joined the effort, a common practice among the tight-knit fishing community that works the dangerous waters of the Bering Sea.

## Crew Size Unclear

The exact number of crew members aboard the vessel has not yet been confirmed. The boat's operating company, which the Coast Guard has not publicly named pending family notifications, is cooperating with investigators.

Alaska's fishing industry, particularly crab and pollock fleets, is considered one of the most dangerous occupations in the United States. The waters surrounding the Aleutian chain are notorious for sudden storms, powerful currents, and rapidly changing weather that can catch even experienced crews off guard.

"This is an incredibly unforgiving stretch of ocean," said John Whiddon, a former commercial fisherman who spent over a decade working Bering Sea crab boats. "Boats go down fast out there, sometimes with very little warning. Every minute matters in a search like this."

## Search to Continue Through the Night

Coast Guard officials said the search would continue through the night and into Thursday, weather permitting.

"We are not giving up hope," Reeves said. "Our crews train for exactly these kinds of conditions, and we will continue searching as long as there is a reasonable chance of finding survivors."

The National Weather Service has issued marine warnings for the region, citing seas up to 15 feet and winds gusting near 40 miles per hour — conditions that could further complicate rescue efforts.

This is a developing story. CNN will provide updates as more information becomes available.

**ADAK, Alaska** — A 623-foot bulk carrier lost engine power in heavy seas near Amchitka Pass early Tuesday morning, drifting perilously close to rocky shoals before a U.S. Coast Guard helicopter crew airlifted all 21 crew members to safety in an operation officials are calling one of the most challenging rescues in the region this year.

The vessel, the *Northern Horizon*, registered under a Marshall Islands flag and operated by Pacific Rim Shipping Group, was en route from Dutch Harbor to Yokohama, Japan, carrying a cargo of grain when its main engine failed around 2:15 a.m. local time. The ship began drifting in 20-foot swells and winds gusting to 45 knots, coming within an estimated three nautical miles of the pass's notoriously rocky shoreline before the crew was evacuated.

"This was a time-sensitive, high-risk situation," said Lt. Cmdr. Sarah Bejarano, spokesperson for the Coast Guard's 17th District in Juneau. "The combination of extreme weather, remote location, and a vessel actively drifting toward shallow water created a very narrow window for a safe rescue. Our aircrew performed magnificently under conditions that pushed the limits of what's operationally possible."

Two MH-60 Jayhawk helicopters were dispatched from Air Station Kodiak, refueling at a forward operating base on Adak before continuing roughly 200 miles to reach the stricken vessel. Crews lowered rescue swimmers to the pitching deck and hoisted crew members in groups of three and four over the course of nearly two hours.

"Conditions were about as bad as we train for," said Coast Guard rescue swimmer Petty Officer 2nd Class Daniel Ruiz, who participated in the operation. "The ship was rolling significantly, and we had limited visibility with the sea spray. But the crew stayed calm and followed instructions, which made all the difference."

All 21 crew members, a mix of Filipino and Ukrainian nationals, were confirmed safe and were transported to Adak for medical evaluation. Coast Guard officials said three crew members were treated for minor injuries, including hypothermia, but none required hospitalization.

The *Northern Horizon* itself remains adrift, though officials say it has stabilized somewhat since the crew's evacuation. A commercial salvage tug dispatched from Dutch Harbor is expected to reach the vessel by Wednesday afternoon, weather permitting.

"Our absolute priority was the safety of the crew, and thanks to the extraordinary work of the U.S. Coast Guard, that objective was met," said Marcus Whitfield, vice president of operations for Pacific Rim Shipping Group, in a statement released from the company's Seattle office. "We are now focused on securing the vessel and mitigating any environmental risk. We are working closely with federal authorities and have contracted a salvage team to stabilize the ship as quickly as safety allows."

Whitfield said the cause of the engine failure was under investigation but that preliminary reports pointed to a mechanical fault in the vessel's fuel system. He added that the ship was carrying approximately 380,000 gallons of heavy fuel oil in addition to its grain cargo, raising concerns about a potential spill should the vessel run aground.

The Coast Guard has classified the incident as a "potential threat to the environment" and has begun coordinating with the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation to monitor the situation. A C-130 aircraft conducted an overflight Tuesday afternoon to assess the vessel's condition and check for any visible sheening in the surrounding waters.

"At this time we have no confirmed reports of a fuel or cargo spill," Bejarano said. "But given the vessel's proximity to sensitive coastal habitat, we're treating this with the seriousness it deserves. Pollution response teams are on standby should conditions change."

Amchitka Pass, located in the western Aleutian Islands, is known among mariners for its unpredictable currents and severe weather, and has been the site of several maritime incidents over the past two decades. The area lies near the Aleutian Islands National Wildlife Refuge, home to significant populations of seabirds, sea otters, and marine mammals.

Local environmental groups have already voiced concern about the potential for ecological damage.

"This is exactly the nightmare scenario people who live and work in these waters have been warning about for years," said Elena Marsh, a spokesperson for the Aleutian Marine Conservation Alliance. "Even a partial fuel release in that ecosystem could have consequences that last for decades."

The National Transportation Safety Board has announced it will open an investigation into the engine failure, examining maintenance records and the vessel's mechanical history. Pacific Rim Shipping Group said it would fully cooperate with investigators.

As of Tuesday evening, the *Northern Horizon* remained approximately four nautical miles offshore, held in place by two support vessels attempting to prevent further drift until the salvage tug arrives. Coast Guard officials said they would continue to monitor the situation around the clock.

"We're not out of the woods yet," Bejarano said. "But the most critical outcome — getting every single crew member home safely — has been achieved. That's what matters most tonight."
